The orientation

Three ideas do most of the work.

You do not need to hold 90 pages in your head. You need a way to read a situation quickly, then choose the safe move. These three ideas are the spine of everything that follows.

01

Keep left. Give way right.

Singapore drives on the left. At an uncontrolled junction, traffic on your right usually goes first. Most right-of-way questions start here.

02

Shape before symbol.

A blue circle commands. A red ring prohibits. A red triangle warns. A rectangle informs. Read the family before you read the detail.

03

Space is the safety system.

Three seconds behind. 1.5 metres past a cyclist. Double the gap when the road is wet. Space buys you time to react.

Read it in order, or use the chapter rail to jump straight to a weak spot. The interactive pieces — sign filter, traffic lights, stopping-distance slider and final quiz — are there to make the facts stick.

Independent study edition · 2026

One caveat before you start: this is a learning companion, not the law. The official handbook and current Traffic Police advisories are always the final word.

Want the source text? Every page of the handbook I started from is preserved in my complete reading copy — with searchable transcripts and the printed tables, signs and diagrams intact.

01

Part A · Driving licences

Know what you’re allowed to drive.

Before the road, the paperwork. The licence ladder is mostly common sense: prove you can drive the class, serve your probation, and keep your points low enough to stay on the road.

Class 2B18+

Motorcycles up to 200cc, or electric motorcycles with a power output up to 15kW.

EntryPass BTT and the Class 2B practical riding test.
Class 2A2B + 1 yr

Motorcycles from 201cc to 400cc, or electric motorcycles from 15.1kW to 25kW.

EntryHold a Class 2B licence for at least one year; pass the 2A practical test.
Class 22A + 1 yr

Motorcycles above 400cc, or electric motorcycles above 25kW.

EntryHold a Class 2A licence for at least one year; pass the Class 2 practical test.
Class 318+

Cars and ambulances up to 3,000kg with no more than seven passengers, excluding the driver. Also light motor tractors.

EntryBTT, Final Theory Test and practical driving test.
Class 3A18+

Automatic cars up to 3,000kg with no more than seven passengers, excluding the driver.

EntrySame test route as Class 3, in an automatic vehicle.
Class 3C / 3CAConversion

Class 3C covers cars up to 3,000kg for eligible work-pass holders converting a foreign licence. Class 3CA is the automatic-only version.

EntryPass BTT. Does not cover light goods vehicles, mini vans or small buses.
Class 421+

Heavy motor cars above 2,500kg, and motor tractors above 2,500kg up to 7,250kg.

EntryHold a Class 3 licence; pass the Class 4 practical test.
Class 4A21+

Omnibuses used for public service, with passengers charged separate fares.

EntryHold a Class 3 licence; pass the Class 4A practical test.
Class 521+

Heavy motor vehicles above 7,250kg that are not constructed to carry passengers.

EntryHold a Class 4 licence; pass the Class 5 practical test.

The baseline for every applicant: at least 18 years old (21 for heavy classes), pass the Basic Theory Test, and be fit to drive — including reading six characters at 25 metres and telling red, amber and green apart.

The route to a licence

Five steps · one year of probation
  1. 01

    Basic Theory Test

    The road-sign, rule and road-safety paper. Everyone starts here.

  2. 02

    Provisional licence

    Your PDL lasts two years. L plates, supervision and third-party insurance are required.

  3. 03

    Final or Riding Theory

    FTT for cars, RTT for motorcycles. Pass before the practical test.

  4. 04

    Practical test

    Cars: within two years of the FTT. Motorcycles: within one year of the RTT.

  5. 05

    Probation

    One year with a probation plate. Thirteen points revokes the new licence.

Provisional licence, in practice Display two 18cm-square L plates — front and rear. Ride or drive only under a qualified instructor’s supervision, and make sure the vehicle is insured against third-party risk. After passing, the probation plate replaces the L plate for one year.

Points, probation, suspension

Driver Improvement Points System
13
points · new driver

Accumulate 13 or more during your one-year probation and your new licence is revoked.

24
points · 24 months

For a driver with no suspension history, 24 points in 24 months triggers a first suspension.

Suspension rules under the Driver Improvement Points System
SuspensionTriggerPeriodAfter retraining
1st24+ points within 24 months12 weeks4 weeks · 1 week if no accident was involved
2nd12+ points within 12 months24 weeks12 weeks
3rd12+ points within 12 months12 monthsNone · licence revoked
4th12+ points within 12 months24 monthsNone · licence revoked
5th+12+ points within 12 months36 monthsNone · licence revoked
Clean slate

12 months, no offences

Your demerit points are expunged after a 12-month offence-free period. A 24-month clean period after suspension also clears the suspension record.

Before you book

12 points max

You cannot book a theory or practical test with more than 12 demerit points, while suspended, or within a year of revocation.

After 65

Medical review

Classes 2B–3CA need certification every three years from 65. Heavy classes need it every year from 65 to 74, plus a proficiency test.

How long it lasts: Singapore citizens and permanent residents hold a lifetime licence. Foreigners on a work pass generally get a licence valid for up to five years, depending on their pass and length of stay.

The appeal route Traffic-offence appeals are made online through the Traffic Police e-Appeals portal. They are considered only on extenuating grounds, with documentary proof. Repeated appeals without fresh evidence will not be considered.
02

Part B · Signs and signals

The road has a vocabulary.

Signs do two jobs: they regulate movement, or they warn and inform. Learn the shape and colour first and you will often know what a sign means before you have read its symbol.

01 / Shape + colour

Read the family first

Blue circle: you must. Red ring: you must not. Red triangle: hazard ahead. Rectangle: information or instruction.

02 / Symbol

Then read the detail

The arrow, number or pictogram tells you the specific direction, limit or hazard. Look for the extra plate underneath.

03 / Context

Then read the road

Time plates, lane markings and where the sign is placed change its meaning. A sign is never just a sticker.

Showing 32 of 32 signs

No sign matches that search. Try “turn”, “speed”, “children” or “tunnel”.

The three-second scan At speed, you do not have time to read. Train your eye to catch the shape and colour first, then the symbol: blue circle = command, red ring = prohibition, red triangle = warning. The details can follow.
Green signs

Directional

Advance signs list destinations; confirmation signs have a chevron and tell you that you are on the right road. Expressway destinations sit in a blue panel.

Electronic signs

EMAS

Travel-time boards use green, amber and red as delays grow. Incident icons flag accidents, congestion, roadworks and lane closures.

Brown signs

Places of interest

Tourist signs are brown with white lettering. Facility signs are usually black on white. They inform; they do not change the rules.

03

Part B · Common road markings

The road writes in lines.

White separates traffic. Yellow restricts parking and stopping. Zig-zags mean “look out.” Once you know the grammar, most marking questions answer themselves.

The 6 / 9 / 3 parking rule

Distance from trouble
6 mFrom an intersection or junction — no parking within six metres.
9 mFrom a bus stop — no parking within nine metres of the stop or bay.
3 mFrom a fire hydrant — no parking within three metres on either side.
Yellow means restriction A single yellow line means no parking 7am–7pm that side, except Sundays and public holidays. Double yellow means no parking at all times, except immediately picking up or dropping off. A single yellow zig-zag is no parking; a double yellow zig-zag is no stopping.

White lines, in one breath: broken white means cross only when safe; continuous white means keep left; double continuous white means do not cross, U-turn or turn right across them. Parking is not allowed beside them either.

04

Part B · Traffic lights

Lights, arrows and human override.

A traffic light is a conversation about who moves next. The safest reading is also the simplest: only go when the signal gives you permission and the road gives you space.

→
Red

Stop.

Come to a complete stop behind the stop line, even if the road looks clear.

At a red arrow, stop in the direction indicated — even when there is no oncoming traffic.

When a person is directing traffic

Higher authority
Follow the officer Signals from a police officer directing traffic take precedence over road signs, traffic lights, markings and traffic regulations. If an officer waves you through a red light, their signal wins. Slow down, make eye contact where possible, and follow the instruction clearly.
Buses only

Green ‘B’

Means go for all buses, so they can pull out of a bus bay or side lane and proceed ahead of other traffic.

Poor visibility

Advanced warning

Flashing amber lights with a “light signals ahead” sign mean the lights are hard to see. Slow down and prepare to stop.

On the road

Intelligent road studs

These blink when the green man comes on. Turning vehicles must watch for them and give way to pedestrians.

Flashing amber means the signals are out of order. Proceed cautiously, treat the junction as uncontrolled, and give way to traffic on your right.

05

Part B · Junctions and right of way

Who goes first?

At a junction without lights, signs or an officer, the give-way rule decides. The default is beautifully boring: slow down, look right, and give way to traffic already on the major road.

The situation

The red car is turning right across the green car’s path. The red car must give way.

Your car Traffic on your right Your intended path
Going straight

Give way to the right

At an uncontrolled junction, give way to traffic going straight across from your right.

Turning right

More people to watch

Give way to oncoming traffic going straight, traffic turning right from your right, and traffic turning left from the opposite direction.

Turning left

Still give way right

Give way to traffic going straight from your right before completing the turn.

Who wins Police officer› Traffic lights› Signs + markings› Give-way rules
Three looks, every time At a junction, look right, then left, then right again. Do not move just because someone behind you is impatient. And do not rely on a signal from an unauthorised person.
Roundabouts Slow down and give way to traffic on your right. Choose your lane before you enter, stay in it around the circle, and leave by the correct exit. Traffic already circulating has priority.

Keep left by default: on a two-lane road, stay left except when overtaking. On a three-lane road, the centre lane is for slower traffic when the left lane is occupied; the outer right lane is for overtaking and emergency vehicles. Do not jump the queue.

Turning geometry: the rear inside wheel tracks closer to the kerb than the front wheel. Leave room for cyclists and pedestrians — and do not let the tail of the vehicle clip the corner.

06

Part B · Speed and space

The gap is the safety feature.

Speed limits tell you the maximum. They do not tell you the safe speed for the rain, the bend, or the child about to step out. The space in front of you is what turns a mistake into a near miss instead of a collision.

50km/h
default limit

Unless otherwise stated, the speed limit on Singapore roads is 50 km/h. Never exceed the limit of the road or your vehicle — whichever is lower.

3 sec

The three-second rule. When the vehicle in front passes a lamp post or sign, count “one-thousand-and-one, one-thousand-and-two, one-thousand-and-three.” If you pass the same point before you finish, you are too close. It replaces the old two-second rule and works at any speed.

Rapid stopping distance / dry road
35metres
At 50 km/h 15m reaction + 20m braking
20406080100
15 m
20 m
Reaction distance: the distance you travel before you even brake Braking distance: the distance while the brakes are working
The wet-road multiplier On a wet road, stopping distance roughly doubles. Braking distance also grows with worn tyres, a fully loaded vehicle, tiredness and alcohol. If you cannot see far enough to stop in the distance ahead, you are out-driving your visibility.

Road-hogging is not harmless. Driving unreasonably slowly in the right or centre lane holds up traffic and pushes other drivers into risky overtakes. If you are not overtaking or turning right, keep left.

The small decisions.

Ten rules that decide whether a drive is forgettable or catastrophic. Learn the verdict first, then the numbers and exceptions around it.

Pass on the right. Only when it is obviously safe.

  • Brow of a hill
  • Across double white lines

The courtesy test: signal early, cancel when done, don’t tailgate, don’t jump the queue, and don’t use the horn to bully. The rules are the floor, not the ceiling.

08

Part B · Special zones and tunnels

When the road changes character.

Some stretches of road are designed around people who are more fragile than a car: children, seniors, pedestrians, cyclists. The speed drops, the paint changes, and the penalties get steeper. Read the room.

Friendly Streets

Neighbourhood pace

Enhanced safety around town centres, markets, schools and MRT stations. Green crossings, gateway signs and traffic-calming features signal that people, not throughput, come first.

40 km/h · care
School Zone

Children are impulsive

Look for the school-zone signs, red road surface and crossings. Slow down, watch for children between parked cars, and be patient at drop-off and pick-up times.

40 km/h · school hours
Silver Zone

More time to cross

Designed for senior pedestrians, with two-stage crossings, narrower lanes, speed humps and 3D markings. Expect longer crossing times and less predictable movement.

Slow · give time
Stiffer penalties inside these zones From 1 July 2021 for Silver and School Zones, and 1 January 2026 for Friendly Streets, specified offences carry an extra 2 demerit points and $100 on top of the usual penalty, capped at a $500 composition fine.
Driving in tunnels

Plan. Light up. Stay in lane.

Before entering: know your route, switch on headlights, tune to the radio, follow the signs, and keep left if you are driving a heavy vehicle. Inside: no stopping, U-turns, reversing, alighting, horn use, tyre changes, refuelling or overtaking.

500 mEscape staircase doors beside the slow lane

If your vehicle breaks down Switch on hazard lights, pull onto the shoulder if possible, and use the nearest SOS phone or call 1800-CALL LTA (1800-2255 582). Stay alert to lane signals and follow the control centre’s instructions.
  1. If there is a fire, use the manual call point and the extinguisher in the emergency cabinet if it is safe to do so.
  2. If you cannot proceed, do not reverse. Switch off the engine, leave the vehicle and head for the nearest exit or escape route.
  3. Escape routes differ: FCT/WVT — head for the entrance or exit; CTE — red-and-white striped doors; KPE/MCE — white doors with green walls.
  4. Approaching a closed tunnel? Do not enter. Follow the variable message signs and take an alternative route.

Work zones

Orange means change

Read the temporary signs

Slow down, obey the temporary speed limit, get into the correct lane early, and don’t weave through cones or barriers. Watch for workers and equipment entering the road.

Respect the TMA

Truck-mounted attenuators are the crash cushions between traffic and workers. They may be stationary or moving slowly. Be patient, keep clear, and change lanes in good time.

09

Part C · Useful information

The life around the car.

Parking, fuel, theft, accidents. These are not edge cases; they are the parts of owning a vehicle that nobody tests you on until the day they matter.

Parking, decoded

Read the signboard at the entrance, not just the lot. HDB and URA car parks use coupon or electronic parking; the board tells you the scheme, hours and charges.

  • Red lots: season parking ticket holders.
  • White lots: outside the Restricted Zone; coupon parking allowed.
  • Red + white: season holders, with coupon parking during restricted hours.
  • Yellow lots: inside the Restricted Zone; higher charges at certain hours.

Eco-driving

The cheapest fuel is a smooth right foot. Eco-driving can cut fuel use by around 10% and reduce emissions — without slowing you down.

  • Don’t idle. Leaving the engine running when stationary can attract a fine of up to $5,000.
  • Check tyre pressure monthly; under-inflated tyres waste fuel.
  • Accelerate and brake gently; keep a steady speed.
  • Use the air-conditioner wisely and remove unnecessary weight.
  • Plan the route before you leave.

Security: lock, look, leave

Most vehicle theft happens in public car parks. Remove the invitation before someone accepts it.

  • Remove ignition keys, lock the handlebar or steering, and take the cashcard.
  • Keep bags, laptops and phones out of sight — preferably in the boot.
  • Park in a well-lit, high-footfall area; avoid dark, secluded corners.
  • Use an alarm, immobiliser or additional lock. On a motorcycle, secure it to something solid.

After a collision

Stay calm, make the scene safe, and protect your claim. The Motor Claims Framework is built around quick, documented reporting.

  • Exchange name, NRIC/FIN, phone, address and insurer with the other parties.
  • Note vehicle numbers and photograph the scene, your vehicle and the other vehicles.
  • Call your insurer’s hotline for a tow truck or advice. Avoid unauthorised tow operators and workshops.
  • Report to an approved reporting centre within 24 hours or the next working day — even if there is no visible damage.

New-ish on the road

Same rules, new machines

Autonomous vehicles

On trial with a yellow beacon. Drive normally: don’t tailgate, keep a safe gap and overtake only when necessary.

Electric motorcycles

Class 2B up to 15kW, 2A from 15.1–25kW, Class 2 above 25kW. No clutch, instant torque — be gentle with the throttle.

Power-assisted bicycles

LTA-approved only, minimum rider age 16, helmet required, registered with a rear plate. No mobile device use while riding.

The last word Passing the test is a milestone. Reading the road is a practice. Keep the gap, keep left, keep looking — and when you are not sure, choose the slower, kinder option. It is almost always the safer one.
